Chapter 8. Embedding Change in Identity: Making New Behaviors Who You Are
Let’s dive into something powerful—how lasting change really happens when it becomes a part of your identity, not just a checklist of things you try to do.
When you start to see yourself as “the kind of person who…”—maybe the kind of person who exercises regularly, leads with empathy, or always looks for creative solutions—it actually reinforces those new habits.
Here’s why identity-based change sticks so much better: it’s not just about setting goals or finding motivation.
Sure, you can plan out your actions, and get inspired, but when your new habit lines up with who you truly believe you are, it starts to feel like the natural choice—almost automatic.
So, how do you help this process along?
Here are a few gentle nudges to build change right into your identity:
First, use language that matches your identity. For example, instead of saying, “I’m trying to run,” what if you simply said, “I’m a runner”?
It sounds small, but it makes a huge difference in how you see yourself.
Next, connect your new behavior to what you truly value. Maybe you want to be more creative, or show more kindness—link those habits to the things that matter most to you, or to your team.
And don’t forget to celebrate those small shifts in identity. When you or your group starts acting in line with this new self-image, recognize it! That little bit of acknowledgment goes a long way.
Think about it this way: a team that puts creativity at the center might regularly share stories about clever problem-solving. Each story reinforces, “This is who we are.”
Or imagine someone who wants to read more often—when they start thinking of themselves as a “reader,” picking up a book instead of scrolling their phone just feels right.
Over time, as you repeat these new behaviors and notice them, they become woven right into your sense of self.
That’s the real magic—when change becomes part of who you are, it’s less likely to fade away, even when your motivation dips or outside support disappears.
So, if you want change to last, let it grow from your identity.
That’s how you make new behaviors stick—not just for a season, but for the long run.
